messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nabil is a 54-year-old married Arab American man who has spent most of his adult life as a community organizer, the kind of person who once moved comfortably through church basements, school auditoriums, and late evening neighborhood meetings, trusting that people could be rallied toward decency. The assault that brought him to treatment happened eight months ago, after an argument with his romantic partner in the partner’s apartment, a place Nabil had entered with the ease of someone who believed he was safe there. The attack turned physical in a darkened hallway near the bedroom after the lights had been switched off in the course of the fight. Nabil remembers being shoved into the wall, struck repeatedly, and trying to orient himself more by sound than sight. What has stayed with him most sharply are not complete images but flashes and noises: his partner’s breathing, the scrape of shoes, the low mechanical thudding from a helicopter passing overhead outside, all of it cut into disconnected pieces. He had trusted this man intimately, and in the weeks after, that betrayal came to dominate the way he understood what had happened: if someone he loved could turn on him there, then the world no longer worked by rules he recognized, and he took the fact that he had stayed in the relationship as proof that something about his own character had invited it.

Those conclusions gave particular force to the things that now set him off. Darkness is not simply unpleasant to him; it feels like the moment when trust failed and ordinary reality gave way. Passing the block where the apartment building stands, or even entering a similarly narrow hallway in one of the community centers where he works, can make him tense before he has consciously registered why. Aircraft sounds are especially potent. During evening canvassing events, when a helicopter circles overhead or a plane cuts low across the city, the sound seems to confirm his sense that danger can descend without warning, and almost instantly he is no longer fully in the present.

When this happens, the memory does not come back as a story. It arrives abruptly and whole in feeling but broken in form, as if he is dropped into fragments he cannot organize. He hears in his head what he heard that night—the pounding overhead, breath, movement in the dark—and for several seconds he struggles to place himself. Sometimes a dark stairwell after a neighborhood meeting will do it; sometimes just walking by the event site on his way to another appointment. The memory itself has made these cues feel broader and less predictable. Because it can be triggered without warning, he has come to experience whole categories of places and sounds as contaminated, always scanning for where the next jolt might come from.

Over the months, Nabil has tried to manage this by becoming relentlessly watchful around other people. At public meetings he positions himself near exits and studies faces as if danger might be legible in a glance or a shift in posture. He has altered his routes to avoid the street where the assault happened, even when that makes him late to organizing events. He has also started wearing loose jackets and long sleeves even in warm weather, wanting to draw less notice to himself, to feel less exposed. These habits make sense to him because the memories feel so immediate; if a place, a sound, or a moment of dim light can bring the assault back in full force, then staying alert and staying away seem like the only reasonable protections.

But those protections have deepened what he believes about himself and other people. Each time he crosses the street to avoid that block, or sits in the back of a meeting room measuring who might be dangerous, it leaves him feeling more certain that the world is fundamentally unsafe and that he has become the sort of man things happen to. The concealing clothing, meant to help him disappear, carries its own private shame; he reads his need for it as evidence of weakness. He has begun to think not only that he was betrayed, but that he should have known better, should have seen who this person really was, and that his failure to do so says something damning about his character.

At work this has narrowed his life. Nabil still shows up, but colleagues have noticed that he avoids evening events in unfamiliar buildings and resists campaigns that would place him near that neighborhood. If a helicopter passes during an outdoor gathering, he momentarily loses track of the conversation and scans the area, already bracing for the memory he fears is coming. That vigilance itself keeps the possibility of danger close; the more he searches people and places for signs of threat, the more readily darkness, certain streets, and overhead aircraft strike him as ominous.

He sought help after his wife told him that although he was physically present at home, he seemed to vanish whenever a sound or place caught him. What frightened him most was not only the memory of the beating, but the sense that it had rewritten his understanding of trust so completely that he might never move through the world normally again. What he hopes, quietly, is not to erase what happened, but to stop living as if every dark hallway, every familiar block, and every sound from the sky means it is happening again.
